teacher-tech-coordinator.title: Teacher & Tech Coordinator

situation.title: The Challenge
situation.content: Title I school with limited technology budget, students who'd never used computers for learning, and teachers skeptical of 'tech for tech's sake.' The school had just received a grant for new computers but no plan for how to actually use them.

approach.title: My Approach
approach.content: Instead of pushing technology on reluctant teachers, I started by understanding their actual pain points. Created simple integrations that solved real problems—like a shared grading system that saved 5 hours per week. Won over skeptics by making their lives easier, not by preaching innovation.
highlights: Started with teacher problems, not technology solutions
Built simple tools before complex systems
Created peer training programs so teachers taught teachers

technical.title: What I Built/Used
technical.content: Basic web-based tools, Google Workspace integrations, simple database for tracking student progress. Nothing fancy—just things that worked reliably.

lessons.title: Key Lessons
lessons.content: The best technology disappears into the workflow. If users have to think about the tool, the tool has failed. Also learned that adoption is a human problem, not a technical one—you can't logic people into using something they don't trust.
takeaways: Technology adoption is a trust problem, not a training problem
Solve real problems, not interesting problems
Meet people where they are, not where you think they should be

suggested_questions: What was the hardest part of getting teachers to adopt new technology?
How did your teaching experience influence your approach to sales later?
What would you do differently if you went back to education today?

sales-development.title: SDR → Account Executive

situation.title: The Challenge
situation.content: Career transition from education to tech with no sales experience, no network in tech, and a resume that screamed 'teacher.' Had to prove I could sell without any track record.

approach.title: My Approach
approach.content: Treated the job search like a sales cycle—researched companies, identified my unique value prop (communication skills + tech comfort), and pitched myself relentlessly. Once in, outworked everyone on activity metrics while learning the craft. Moved from SDR to AE in 18 months.
highlights: Reframed teaching experience as 'presentation and persuasion' skills
Hit 150% of activity metrics while learning
Built internal champions who advocated for my promotion

technical.title: What I Learned
technical.content: Full sales tech stack—CRM, prospecting tools, sales engagement platforms. More importantly, learned the entire B2B sales cycle from cold outreach to closed deal.

lessons.title: Key Lessons
lessons.content: Discovered that enterprise sales is really just teaching with higher stakes. The same skills that worked in a classroom—breaking down complex ideas, reading the room, adjusting on the fly—work in a boardroom. Career changes are about reframing, not restarting.
takeaways: Skills transfer more than job titles suggest
Enterprise sales is teaching with a quota

suggested_questions: How did you make the transition from teaching to tech sales?
What surprised you most about enterprise sales?
What skills from teaching do you still use today?

tableau-ae.title: Account Executive

situation.title: The Challenge
situation.content: Selling complex data visualization software to enterprises that often didn't understand their own data problems. Competition from Microsoft Power BI was intensifying. Had to differentiate on value, not price.

approach.title: My Approach
approach.content: Positioned myself as a data strategy consultant, not a software salesperson. Spent more time understanding how organizations actually made decisions than demoing features. Built relationships with data teams AND business leaders—the rare AE who could speak both languages.
highlights: Led with business outcomes, not product features
Built technical credibility through Tableau certifications
Created custom demos that mirrored each client's actual data challenges

technical.title: Technical Depth
technical.content: Became genuinely proficient in Tableau—not just demo-level, but could build real dashboards. This credibility with data teams opened doors that pure salespeople couldn't access.

lessons.title: Key Lessons
lessons.content: Most companies have more data than insight. The gap between data collection and data-driven decisions is human, not technical. Also learned that technical credibility—even at a basic level—opens doors that pure sales skills cannot.
takeaways: Data problems are usually people problems
Speak the language of both data teams and executives

suggested_questions: What did you learn about how organizations actually use data?
How did you compete against Microsoft's bundled offerings?
What made your approach different from other Tableau salespeople?

tableau-am.title: Enterprise Account Manager

situation.title: The Challenge
situation.content: Promoted to manage strategic accounts worth $2M+ annually. These weren't sales cycles—they were relationships. Had to expand existing deployments while navigating Salesforce's acquisition of Tableau, which created uncertainty among customers.

approach.title: My Approach
approach.content: Became a genuine partner to my accounts, not a vendor. Spent time understanding their internal politics, helped them build business cases for expansion, and positioned myself as their advocate inside Salesforce. During the acquisition, proactively addressed concerns before they became objections.
highlights: Built executive relationships at VP+ level across all accounts
Created 'value realization' frameworks that documented ROI
Navigated acquisition uncertainty by over-communicating and under-promising

technical.title: Organizational Navigation
technical.content: At this level, the 'technology' is organizational dynamics. Learned to map stakeholder landscapes, identify hidden blockers, and build consensus across competing priorities. Also deepened Salesforce platform knowledge.

lessons.title: Key Lessons
lessons.content: Enterprise deals aren't won in meetings—they're won between meetings. The real work is helping your champions sell internally. Also learned that retention is about value delivery, not relationship management. If they're not using the product well, relationships don't matter.
takeaways: Your champion isn't the deal—the organization is
Win between meetings, not in them
Retention is about value delivery, not relationship management

suggested_questions: How did you navigate the Salesforce acquisition?
What does 'Account Manager of the Year' actually mean?
What's your approach to managing large enterprise accounts?
Tell me about a deal you lost and what you learned.

juniper-square.title: Senior Account Manager

situation.title: The Challenge
situation.content: Moved from a large company (Salesforce) to a growth-stage fintech. Smaller team, more ownership, higher expectations for individual contribution. Also: learning an entirely new industry (real estate investment) from scratch.

approach.title: My Approach
approach.content: Rapid industry immersion—read everything, talked to everyone, became genuinely knowledgeable about real estate investment operations. Also started building internal tools to automate repetitive parts of my job, which sparked my interest in AI tooling.
highlights: Built internal automation tools that saved 10+ hours/week
Identified product gaps that led to new feature development

technical.title: Beginning to Build
technical.content: This is where I started coding for real. Built automation scripts to handle routine tasks, created reporting tools for my accounts, and started experimenting with AI APIs for content generation.

lessons.title: Key Lessons
lessons.content: Discovered that I was more interested in building the tools than closing the deals. Also learned that smaller companies offer more surface area for impact—you can actually change things, not just work within them.
takeaways: Building tools is more interesting than using tools
Smaller companies = more leverage for individual contribution
The best way to understand a problem is to build a solution for it

suggested_questions: Why did you leave a big company for a startup?
What automation tools did you build and why?
How did this role lead to your transition to AI building?

ai-builder.title: AI Builder & Tools Creator

situation.title: The Challenge
situation.content: Made the leap to full-time building after realizing that my side projects were more energizing than my day job. No external funding, no team—just skills I'd been developing and problems I wanted to solve.

approach.title: My Approach
approach.content: Building in public, learning by shipping. Started with problems I personally experienced—voice capture for ideas (DailyScribe), accelerated learning (ALOS), content generation from structured data (Art of Fact). Each project teaches me new skills while solving real problems.

technical.title: Current Stack
technical.content: Python for backend, JavaScript for frontend, Gemini/OpenAI APIs for AI capabilities. Learning system design and architecture through building increasingly complex projects. Still early, but improving rapidly.

lessons.title: Key Lessons (So Far)
lessons.content: Building something that works is very different from building something that scales. Also learning that solo building requires discipline—no team means no accountability except yourself. Still learning. That's the point.

suggested_questions: What are you building right now?
How do you prioritize what to learn?
What's the hardest part of building alone?
What's your ideal next role?
